summary.one_line: A Kolkata-founded, US-run, acquisition-built call-centre/CX outsourcer whose profits and cash flow have genuinely inflected (FY26 PAT Rs 169.8 cr, operating cash flow Rs 264 cr), but with no real moat, AI-substitution risk, a governance file (ROC shell-company inquiry, promoter-entity loans, a past director disqualification) and promoters selling down from a ~Rs 0.12/share cost -- worth tracking, not applying to.
bull_points: Profit and margins have inflected: revenue from operations rose from Rs 991.3 cr (FY24) to Rs 1,818.1 cr (FY26) while PAT rose from Rs 36.3 cr to Rs 169.8 cr and EBITDA margin (ex-other income) went from 7.5% to 16.3% (S2, S3).
Profits are backed by cash: operating cash flow was Rs 264.2 cr in FY26 against PAT of Rs 169.8 cr, and receivable days fell from 94 (FY24) to about 76 (FY26) (S2, S3).
Most of the fresh money de-levers the company: Rs 275.7 cr of the Rs 500 cr fresh issue repays borrowings that stood at Rs 266.9 cr in March 2026 and Rs 238.1 cr in June 2026 (S3, S8).

A genuinely global multi-shore network -- 40 delivery centres in 13 countries, 28 languages, 208 customers including 22 Fortune 1000 names -- gives onshore, nearshore and offshore price points to US clients (S2, S8).
bear_points: No real moat: this is a people-heavy BPO where employee costs are about 66% of revenue and voluntary attrition is ~26-32%, competing against far larger players such as Teleperformance, Concentrix and Firstsource (S1, S14).

Growth is acquisition-led and hard to separate from organic: six acquisitions since 2024 and 16 since 2007; revenue actually fell 10.3% in FY24 before acquisitions resumed, and goodwill rose from Rs 87.6 cr to Rs 362.2 cr in two years (S1, S2, S3).

Governance flags in the DRHP: ROC West Bengal notices (2021-2023) sought clarification on 'involvement in shell companies' and an alleged section 129 contravention, the CEO's DIN was suspended 2017-2019 for non-filing at another company, and the company lent to promoter-group entities (S1).
Promoters hold shares at a weighted cost of Rs 0.12-0.13 and are taking out Rs 202 cr via the OFS plus a further Rs 120 cr via pre-IPO secondary sales at Rs 289 (S1, S8, S10).
Customer concentration is rising: top 5/top 10 customers were ~39%/~49% of FY26 revenue versus 29%/41% in FY24, and US-Canada is now ~85% of revenue (S1, S2, S13).
watch_points: Whether the ROC West Bengal inquiry on shell-company involvement (reply filed February 2024, no update at DRHP date) produces any order (S1).
Organic growth once the FY25-26 acquisitions (S4 Communications, Sequential, Scribe.ology, Skycom, VA Platinum) are in the base -- Q1 FY27 revenue was Rs 490.5 cr (S3, S2).
Q1 FY27 operating cash flow of Rs 23.2 cr was well below Q1 PAT of Rs 55.7 cr while receivables rose to Rs 409.9 cr -- watch whether the FY26 cash conversion holds (S3).
Use of the ~Rs 163 cr earmarked for unidentified acquisitions and general corporate purposes (S8, S2).

reasoning: The money raised mostly helps the balance sheet, not the business: of Rs 702 cr, Rs 202 cr is OFS going to promoter holding companies, Rs 275.7 cr repays debt, only Rs 61.15 cr funds the AI tools (Arya, MindVoice), and ~Rs 163 cr is a blank cheque for unidentified acquisitions and general purposes (S8, S2, S5). Promoters also sold Rs 120 cr pre-IPO at the issue price from a Rs 0.12-0.13 cost base (S1, S10).

There is no defensible moat: the business is labour-arbitrage CX with employee cost ~66% of revenue, 26-32% attrition, short contracts (mostly under 24 months, some terminable without penalty) and generative-AI risk that the company's own DRHP and industry consultant flag as a direct threat to agent-based work (S1, S14).

The quality of the profit improvement is real but young: PAT went from Rs 36 cr to Rs 170 cr in two years with strong FY26 cash conversion (CFO Rs 264 cr), yet it followed a revenue decline in FY24 and coincided with six acquisitions, a low ~10% effective tax rate in FY26 and goodwill reaching ~65% of net worth -- one strong year is not yet a track record (S3, S2, S1).

Governance needs more time to earn trust: the DRHP discloses ROC notices on shell-company involvement, a past DIN suspension of the CEO, a 2013 RBI FEMA penalty, two insolvency petitions by operational creditors, and recurring loans/outsourcing/rent with promoter-group entities such as Window Technologies, PKR Services and SSR Services (S1, S4).

Risks that matter are concentrated in the same direction: ~85% US-Canada revenue, rising top-10 customer share (~49%), no FX hedging, and US anti-offshoring sentiment (S1, S2, S13). A few listed quarters showing organic growth, sustained cash conversion and clean resolution of the ROC matter would justify revisiting; on today's evidence it is a track, not an invest.

subsections.title: What Fusion CX actually does and how it earns money

blocks.text: Fusion CX is a contact-centre and customer-experience (CX) outsourcer: it runs customer acquisition (lead generation, tele-sales), customer service (inbound/outbound queries), order fulfilment support, payments and collections, customer retention, technical support and 'digital solutions' (content moderation, data annotation) for client companies over voice, email, chat, social media and messaging (S1). It was incorporated in Kolkata on 25 February 2004 as Xplore-Tech Services and renamed Fusion CX in 2024 (S5). In the RHP period it has added 'AI data infrastructure services' such as data collection, annotation and robot teleoperation (S2, S8).

Revenue is earned under fixed-fee, transaction-based and outcome-based contracts (S1). In practice this is a seat- and headcount-driven business: employee benefits expense was Rs 1,193.0 cr in FY26 against revenue from operations of Rs 1,818.1 cr, i.e. about 66% of revenue, consistent with the 66-69% range disclosed for FY22-9MFY25 (S3, S1). Contracts typically run 3-60 months with the majority under 24 months, and many can be terminated on short notice without penalty (S1).

blocks.caption: Revenue by service line (Rs cr; DRHP restated, latest service split available)

blocks.text: The 'AI' label is mostly a wrapper around a classic BPO: digital solutions were only ~4.5-5.8% of revenue, while voice-heavy customer service and acquisition make up roughly two-thirds (S1, S2).

The company had 208 customers including 22 Fortune 1000 companies as of June 2026 (S8). Named clients in the DRHP include DMEC Capital Services, Telaid, Achieve Collection, Ameriflex, Coastline, Ajio, Meesho, Arvind Fashion, Propneu, Leonardo Hotels, Insurance Express and Traya (S1). Concentration is meaningful and rising: top 5/top 10 customers were 29.1%/41.0% of FY24 revenue and about 39%/49% of FY26 revenue (S1, S2).

Telecom and utilities is the anchor vertical, rising from 15.7% of revenue in FY22 to 30.9% in FY24 and 47.3% in FY26, helped by the S4 Communications and Sequential Technology acquisitions; HTT (high-tech, growth, travel), BFSI, healthcare and retail are each roughly 12-14% (S1, S2). By customer geography, US and Canada rose to 85.3% of FY26 revenue from 75.3% in FY25, with India falling to 11.3% from 19.4% (S13).

Average relationship length with the top 5 customers is 11.3 years (S1), but the multibagg summary of the offer document notes that top customers terminated contracts in FY24 -- the year revenue fell 10.3% (S5, S1).

subsections.title: Operating model: delivery network, people and acquisitions

blocks.text: Delivery runs from 40 centres across 13 countries (June 2026) in a multi-shore model: onshore centres in the USA and Canada for compliance-heavy work; nearshore centres in Jamaica, Colombia, El Salvador, Belize, Mexico, Morocco, Albania and Kosovo; and offshore centres in India (Kolkata, Howrah, Durgapur, Siliguri, Gurugram, Noida, Mohali, Bengaluru, Mumbai), the Philippines, Indonesia and Thailand (S1, S8). US headquarters are in Norcross, Georgia; both executive promoters live in Georgia, USA (S1). All delivery centres are leased, the Kolkata head office is sub-leased from promoter-group company Window Technologies, and at the DRHP date the UK centre operated out of an employee's premises (S1).

Headcount was ~13,735 CX employees plus ~3,829 field workforce at June 2026 (S8, S2). The field workforce -- used on Indian telecom/utility on-site tasks such as electricity-board billing -- was 12,323 in December 2024, so that low-value line has shrunk sharply (S1). Voluntary attrition among CX staff ran at 28.6-32.2% through FY22-9MFY25 (S1).

Technology sits in subsidiary Omind (Omind Technologies Inc. and its Indian arm), which builds Arya (agent co-pilot and QA), MindVoice (conversational AI) and Mind WorkPlace (workforce management); the company also resells third-party tools such as MindSpeech accent harmonisation from sanas.ai (S1). R&D spend was Rs 15.4 cr in FY24 (1.55% of revenue) (S1).

blocks.caption: Recent acquisitions (DRHP and ICICI Direct)
rows: Telecom, healthcare payer and energy CX; US/India/Philippines centres
Named by ICICI Direct among six deals since 2024

blocks.text: The company-commissioned Everest Group report values the global CX market at about Rs 30.53 trillion (US$370 bn) in 2024, with outsourced CX about 32% of the market in 2023-24 (S1). The 'outsourced digital CX' slice is put at Rs 1,409.79 bn in 2024, projected to reach Rs 1,917.26 bn by 2027 at a 10.79% CAGR, slower than the 14.05% CAGR of 2021-24 (S1).

The same report lists the headwinds plainly: enterprise automation with voice AI and generative AI 'poses a potential threat' to the CX industry and may reduce reliance on human agents; macro slowdowns cut CX budgets; and wage inflation in delivery hubs erodes margins (S1). The DRHP adds anti-outsourcing legislation and sentiment in the US as a risk to pricing and volumes (S1).
The industry data is paid for by the company (Everest was engaged in December 2024 for the offer) and should be read as context, not independent validation (S1).

subsections.title: Competitors and whether there is a moat

blocks.text: Fusion CX competes with global giants that are themselves consolidating -- the DRHP cites Concentrix's acquisition of Webhelp and Teleperformance's acquisition of Majorel in 2023 and Firstsource's acquisition of Ascensos in 2024 -- and with a long tail of regional and unorganised call-centre operators (S1). The Indian listed peers used by analysts are Firstsource and Sagility (S14). At ~Rs 1,818 cr of revenue (S3) Fusion CX is a small player in this field.

items: No import-substitution, licence or regulatory barrier: the DRHP itself says the BPO and CX industry is 'saturated with regional and global providers that compete aggressively on pricing' and larger firms 'pose a significant threat' to its share (S1).

No market-share claim of note: the DRHP makes no claim to be a leader in any segment; the main external endorsement cited is a Frost & Sullivan 2025 'technology innovation leadership' recognition (S1).
IP is thin: the core platforms are unpatented and the logo is not registered in India; the registered mark is held by US subsidiary O'Currance (S1).
Real but replicable strengths: a multi-shore footprint in 13 countries, 28 languages, and long relationships (11.3 years average with the top 5) give some switching friction (S1, S8).

blocks.text: Plainly: there is no structural moat. Sushil Finance characterises it as a people-intensive BPO/CX business with limited structural moats, and the company's own disclosures support that reading (S14, S1).

Fusion CX is positioning Omind's Arya, MindVoice and Mind WorkPlace as its route from a 'traditional CX service provider into a productized, SaaS-enabled CX service provider' (S1). It spent Rs 15.4 cr in FY24 and Rs 13.9 cr in 9MFY25 on generative-AI CX technology development, and Rs 61.15 cr of IPO money is earmarked for these tools (S1, S8).

The flip side is that generative AI directly attacks the routine voice and chat volumes that make up most of Fusion's revenue; the DRHP warns customers 'may develop in-house capabilities' that reduce their need for its services, and ICICI Direct lists AI-led automation reducing voice volumes as a key risk (S1, S2). Digital solutions remain only about 4.5% of revenue (S2), so the AI transition is still largely a plan rather than a revenue line.

The DRHP covers FY22-9MFY25; the October 2026 RHP updates restated figures to FY24-FY26 and Q1 FY27. The RHP figures below come from secondary summaries of the RHP (multibagg, ICICI Direct, Chittorgarh, IPO Watch) because the RHP PDF could not be retrieved directly; FY24 figures match across the DRHP and those summaries (S1, S2, S3, S6, S8).

Sources: FY22-FY24 from the DRHP (S1); FY24-FY26 revenue, PAT and Q1 from multibagg's RHP summary (S3); EBITDA ex-other income from ICICI Direct (S2); FY25 EBITDA incl. other income from Sushil Finance (Rs 197.78 cr) and ThePrint/PTI (FY26 Rs 329.87 cr, up 66.8%) (S14, S13).

The trend is genuinely positive but it is not a smooth growth story. Revenue fell 10.3% in FY24 and EBITDA fell for two years running before FY25 (S1). The FY25-FY26 rebound coincides with S4 (Dec 2024), Sequential (Jan 2025) and Scribe.ology (Apr 2025), so a large part of the 35% two-year revenue CAGR is bought, not organic (S1, S2). Margin expansion is the more impressive part: EBITDA margin ex-other income more than doubled from 7.5% to 16.3% (S2).

Tax is unusually low: FY25 tax was Rs 3.4 cr on PBT of Rs 77.7 cr and FY26 tax Rs 19.5 cr on PBT of Rs 189.3 cr (~10%) (S3). A normalising tax rate would take a visible bite out of reported PAT growth.

subsections.title: Balance sheet health and cash conversion

blocks.caption: Balance sheet and cash flow (Rs cr)

blocks.text: Sources: net worth, borrowings and assets from Chittorgarh (S6); receivables, goodwill and cash flows from multibagg's RHP summary (S3); the leverage ratio is computed here as borrowings divided by net worth from S6 (Chittorgarh's own reported debt/equity is 0.53 for March 2026 and 0.51 for June 2026, likely including other liabilities) (S6). Lease liabilities of Rs 135.6 cr at March 2026 sit on top of bank debt, and cash was Rs 89.6 cr (S3).

FY26 cash conversion was strong: operating cash flow of Rs 264.2 cr exceeded PAT of Rs 169.8 cr, after a weaker FY24 (CFO Rs 39.3 cr on PAT Rs 36.3 cr) (S3). ICICI Direct puts receivable days at about 76 in FY26 versus 94 in FY24 (S2). However, Q1 FY27 CFO was only Rs 23.2 cr against Q1 PAT of Rs 55.7 cr, and receivables kept rising to Rs 409.9 cr; IPO Watch's reviewer flags rising receivables as a concern (S3, S8).

Goodwill of Rs 362.2 cr is about 65% of March 2026 net worth of Rs 552.5 cr (S3, S6). The DRHP already lists goodwill and intangibles as the company's largest assets and impairment as a risk (S1). Also note Kotak Neo reports consolidated debt of Rs 322 cr as of August 2026, higher than the June figure, which suggests borrowings were drawn again after June (S9).

subsections.title: Does the trend support the growth story?

items: Supportive: two consecutive years of 34-37% revenue growth, margin expansion of ~9 points, RoNW up from 13.4% to 30.3%, and real operating cash in FY26 (S2, S3).

Less supportive: the FY24 revenue decline shows the base is volatile and client-dependent; growth since then leans on acquisitions, which ICICI Direct notes explicitly ('the base was low and growth has leaned on acquisitions') (S1, S2).
Mixed: Q1 FY27 revenue of Rs 490.5 cr annualises to a run-rate above FY26, and PAT margin of 11.4% is higher, but Q1 cash conversion was weak (S3).
Dividends of 10%/20%/30% of face value in FY24-FY26 are token at a Re 1 face value (S8).

blocks.text: Bottom line on financials: genuine improvement, credible FY26 cash, moderate leverage -- but one strong year after an acquisition spree is not yet proof of a durable organic growth engine.

sections.title: Issue details and objects of the issue

blocks.caption: Key offer terms
rows: Rs 202 cr, ~69.9 lakh shares; Rs 101 cr each by P N S Business and Rasish Consultants (S7, S9)
Anchor 13 Oct; open 14-16 Oct; allotment 19 Oct; listing 22 Oct 2026 on BSE/NSE (S9)
Nuvama, IIFL Capital, Motilal Oswal / KFin Technologies (S8)

blocks.text: The issue was cut from Rs 1,000 cr (Rs 600 cr fresh + Rs 400 cr OFS) in the May 2025 DRHP to Rs 702 cr; SEBI cleared the draft in December 2025 (S1, S18, S12, S9). In the week before the IPO the two promoter entities also sold 41.52 lakh shares for Rs 120 cr at Rs 289 to Kotak Mahindra Life Insurance, Ashish Kacholia and Mukul Agrawal-backed Sanshi Fund-I (S10).

blocks.caption: Use of the Rs 500 cr fresh issue (RHP, per secondary summaries)
rows: Repayment/prepayment of borrowings of the company and certain subsidiaries
Investment in step-down subsidiaries Omind Technologies Inc. and Omind Technologies Pvt Ltd to upgrade Arya and MindVoice
Unidentified acquisitions, strategic initiatives and general corporate purposes

blocks.text: Figures from IPO Watch, multibagg and ICICI Direct; ICICI Direct notes the acquisitions/GCP bucket is capped at 35% of gross proceeds (S8, S5, S2). In the DRHP the equivalent amounts were Rs 291.9 cr for debt and Rs 74.7 cr for Omind, the latter phased Rs 19.4 cr / 25.1 cr / 30.2 cr over FY26-FY28 (S1); the RHP deployment schedule for the reduced Rs 61.15 cr could not be verified.

The DRHP states no acquisition target has been identified and no definitive agreement signed for the inorganic-growth money (S1). Investors are funding a blank cheque for a strategy that has already produced most of the recent growth and most of the goodwill.

subsections.title: What the money does for the investor

blocks.text: Of the Rs 702 cr, Rs 202 cr (29%) never reaches the company -- it goes to the promoters' holding companies (S9). Adding the Rs 120 cr pre-IPO secondary, promoters are realising about Rs 322 cr at Rs 289 per share against a weighted average acquisition cost of Rs 0.12-0.13 per share (S10, S1).

Debt repayment of Rs 275.7 cr against borrowings of Rs 238-267 cr (June/March 2026) would make the company close to bank-debt-free and should save most of the Rs 45.5 cr FY26 finance cost (part of which is lease interest) (S3, S6, S2). That is a real but one-off EPS uplift; only Rs 61.15 cr goes into the technology that is supposed to differentiate the business (S8).
Net assessment: a balance-sheet clean-up plus promoter liquidity event, with a modest AI budget and an acquisition war chest -- not a capex-led growth raise.

Promoters are Pankaj Dhanuka (55, Chairman, MD and CEO, a US national resident in Georgia) and Kishore Saraogi (56, COO and MD, non-resident Indian also in Georgia), plus their holding companies P N S Business Pvt Ltd (99.99% owned by Dhanuka) and Rasish Consultants Pvt Ltd (99.99% owned by Saraogi); together they held 99.28% at the DRHP date (S1). The two co-founded the company in 2004 and have 21 and 26 years respectively in BPO/CX (S1).

The board at the DRHP date had eight members: two executive promoters, two non-executive non-independent directors (Ritesh Chakraborty and Bradley Tyler Call, both US-based and appointed May 2025) and four independent directors appointed from December 2024 onward, including Kashi Prasad Khandelwal and Saagarika Ghoshal (S1). Because both MDs are non-residents, their appointment required Central Government approval, which was pending at the DRHP date (S1).

items: Dhanuka's DIN was suspended from September 2017 to December 2019 because Bee-Cee Tubes Pvt Ltd, where he was a director, failed to file financial statements for three years; it was restored under the condonation scheme (S1).
Dhanuka sits on the boards of promoter-group companies Global Seamless Tubes & Pipes, GSTP (HFS) and PKR Services Inc., businesses unrelated to CX that also transact with Fusion CX (S1).
Promoter remuneration: Dhanuka Rs 4.71 cr and Saraogi Rs 4.40 cr in 9MFY25 (S1).

blocks.text: The RPT section is not routine. Promoter-group company Window Technologies is landlord of the Kolkata head office (Rs 0.78 m/month), was paid Rs 23.6 cr in FY23 and Rs 16.2 cr in FY22 for outsourcing work (2.1-2.2% of revenue), receives loans from Fusion CX (Rs 10.0 cr in FY22, Rs 3.6 cr in FY23, Rs 2.0 cr in 9MFY25) and pays dividends to Fusion CX on preference shares (S1). In 9MFY25 Fusion CX also lent Rs 19.1 cr to PKR Services Inc. and Rs 6.0 cr to SSR Services Inc., both promoter-linked US entities (S1).

blocks.caption: Related-party loans outstanding incl. interest (RHP, per multibagg)

blocks.text: Balances have been brought down ahead of listing, but multibagg notes the RHP gives no interest rates, maturities or security for these loans, asserts arm's-length terms without support, and shows a naming inconsistency between 'Window Technologies' and 'Windstream Telecommunications' (S4). Fusion CX also paid professional-service fees to SSR Services Inc. (Rs 6.7 cr in FY24) and GSTP (HFS) (Rs 5.5 cr in FY24), and sold equipment worth Rs 7.3 cr to Omind before acquiring it (S1).

A listed company lending to and buying services from its promoters' other private businesses is the kind of pattern that deserves scrutiny after listing; the amounts are small relative to revenue (mostly 0.1-2%), but they are recurring and two-directional (S1, S4).

items: ROC West Bengal sent notices in April 2021, September 2023 and December 2023 under section 206 seeking information on borrowings, investments, share issues and bank accounts, an alleged contravention of section 129, and clarification on 'involvement in shell companies, including on certain financial activities in connection with such shell companies'; directors were summoned in September 2023, and the company replied in October 2023 and February 2024 with no further update at the DRHP date (S1).
RBI imposed a Rs 0.10 m penalty in January 2013 for non-filing of form ODI on a remittance to an overseas joint venture (S1).
Two operational creditors (Parsvatech Workspaces, Devansh Logistics) have filed IBC petitions against the company before NCLT Kolkata, not yet admitted at the DRHP date (S1).

Outstanding litigation at the DRHP date: 4 criminal, 8 tax, 1 regulatory and 4 material civil cases against the company (Rs 16.9 cr); claims of Rs 31.7 cr against subsidiaries excluding a US suit by Steven Brown and others against Ameridial and Sequential; and 9 criminal proceedings against directors (S1).
Mobikwik owes the company Rs 1.8 cr under dispute (S1).

blocks.text: Individually most of these are small, but together -- a shell-company inquiry by the ROC, a past director disqualification, promoter-entity loans and creditor insolvency petitions -- they make governance the weakest part of the case. Whether the RHP reports any change in the ROC matter could not be verified (S1).

items: AI substitution of the core product: routine voice and chat work, most of Fusion's revenue, is what generative and voice AI automate; the company's own industry report calls this a potential threat, and clients may take work in-house (S1, S2).
Customer and market concentration: top 10 customers ~49% of FY26 revenue and US-Canada ~85%; contracts are mostly under 24 months and some can be terminated without penalty (S2, S13, S1).
Acquisition dependence and integration: future acquisitions are 'key' to the growth strategy, ~Rs 163 cr is set aside without targets, and goodwill is already ~65% of net worth (S1, S3, S6).
Labour economics: employee cost ~66% of revenue and 28-32% attrition mean wage inflation or a hiring squeeze flows straight to margins (S1, S3).

blocks.text: These four are inter-linked: if AI erodes voice volumes at a large US telecom client, the company loses revenue concentrated in one vertical (telecom/utilities ~47%) and one market, and would be tempted to buy growth again (S2).

items: Governance: ROC inquiry on shell-company involvement, related-party loans to promoter entities, and the CEO's past DIN suspension (S1, S4).
Currency: ~74% of revenue is in USD and the company had no hedging arrangements at the DRHP date; multi-year fixed-price contracts mean rupee appreciation hits margins (S1, S2).
Data security and privacy: the business handles health, payment-card and personal data under HIPAA, GDPR, CCPA and India's DPDP Act; a breach could cause penalties and client loss (S1).
Cash-conversion reversal: Q1 FY27 operating cash flow of Rs 23.2 cr vs PAT of Rs 55.7 cr, with receivables up again (S3).
Tax normalisation: FY26 effective tax of ~10% looks unsustainably low for a profitable group (S3).

blocks.text: The DRHP's boilerplate risks (pandemics, macro, general competition) are omitted here; the list above is what could actually change the investment decision.

On the FY26 results (August 2026), CEO Pankaj Dhanuka attributed the profit jump to execution, revenue growth, operating efficiencies and cost discipline and said the company is 'focused on scaling our AI-led customer experience capabilities'; Kishore Saraogi said the results position it for 'the next phase of growth' (S13). The company also announced a planned Rs 100 cr investment over three years in an IT/ITeS campus at Bengal Silicon Valley Tech Hub, New Town, Kolkata (S13).

The offer document's stated strategy is (i) continued acquisitions to add geographies, verticals and services, (ii) productising Omind's AI tools to move towards a 'SaaS-enabled' CX model, and (iii) new service lines such as AI data annotation and teleoperation (S1, S2). The DRHP also mentions plans for a manufacturing unit for SMC (sheet moulding compound) products for power companies -- an unrelated diversification (S1).
No numerical revenue or margin guidance was found in the sources reviewed. Any growth expectation beyond FY26 would be inference from history, not a management commitment.

Near term, debt repayment should lift reported profit through lower interest, and Q1 FY27 already showed an 11.4% PAT margin on Rs 490.5 cr revenue (S3). The bigger question is whether AI tools become paid products or simply protect existing seats at lower prices; with digital solutions at ~4.5% of revenue (S2), the evidence for the former is thin so far.

items: Positive marker to watch: organic growth excluding FY25-26 acquisitions, and growth in digital/AI revenue share above ~5% (S2).
Negative marker to watch: further large acquisitions funded by debt soon after listing, or rising related-party balances (S1, S4).

subsections.title: Anchor book, day-1 status and grey market

blocks.text: The anchor book on 13 October 2026 raised about Rs 315-316 cr by allotting 1.09 cr shares at Rs 289, the top of the band (S10, S7). Named anchors include Kotak Mahindra Life Insurance, Ashish Kacholia-backed Bengal Finance and Investment, Natixis Investment Managers and Meru Investment Fund PCC-Cell 1; domestic mutual funds -- Kotak, ICICI Prudential, Motilal Oswal, Quant, ITI and JM Financial -- took 77.84% of the anchor portion through 15 schemes (S10, S11). Anchor lock-in end dates were not stated in the sources reviewed.

This report is written on 14 October 2026, the first day of bidding. No category-wise (QIB/NII/retail) subscription figures had been published in any source found; trackers showed placeholders of 0x or 'not yet available' (S15, S17, S19). Day-1 numbers, when they appear, will be partial and QIB books usually fill on the last day.

GMP is an unofficial, unregulated indicator that has swung between Rs 19 and Rs 55 in five days (S15). It says nothing about the business and is not a basis for this report's call. Strong anchor names reflect institutional appetite at the issue price, not a verdict on the governance issues above.

method: Primary source: the Fusion CX DRHP dated 26 May 2025, downloaded from the company's investor page and read directly for the offer summary, risk factors (1-32), business, industry overview (Everest Group report), promoters, board, related-party transactions and litigation summary (S1). The RHP dated 8 October 2026 was located (S16) but every copy (ipowatch, chittorgarh, Nuvama) exceeded the fetch size limit or returned 403, so RHP-period figures (FY25, FY26, Q1 FY27 P&L, balance sheet, cash flow, objects, RPT loan balances) were taken from secondary summaries of the RHP and cross-checked across at least two of: ICICI Direct (S2), multibagg (S3, S4, S5), Chittorgarh (S6), IPO Watch (S8), Sushil Finance (S14) and PTI/ThePrint (S13).
